title: The Secrets to a Healthy Old Age

blanks.sentence: Ageing is partly linked to the _____ of the body's cells.
Earlier explanations focused mainly on _____ processes; newer research also considers how people live in society.
A recent paper suggests that _____ of ageing can be influenced by how people live.
Alongside diet, a _____ may matter for health in later life.
Researchers followed _____ over their lives to examine differences in health.
Older people may feel _____, which can have a serious effect on health.
The impact of this isolation is compared with that of _____.
In Mediterranean countries, the climate encourages _____ outdoors.
People may share _____ and live with family members of different generations.
Wherever people live, keeping in _____ with other people may help them age well.

multipleChoice.question: What is the main change in researchers' understanding of ageing described in the discussion?
options: They now see ageing as completely preventable through medical treatment.
They now consider social and lifestyle factors alongside changes in cells.
They now regard inherited traits as less important than a person's age.
They now believe the body's cells remain unchanged during later life.

multipleChoice.question: What does the figure from the recent paper suggest about ageing?
options: A substantial share may be influenced by the way people live.
Most people will remain healthy until the age of sixty.
Lifestyle explains every difference between older people.
Cell changes account for exactly sixty per cent of ageing.

multipleChoice.question: What did the twin studies described by Professor Harper do?
options: Keep the twins' diets identical throughout adulthood.
Compare medical treatments given after retirement.
Measure participants' attitudes in a single short interview.
Follow twins over time and compare their outlook with later health.

multipleChoice.question: According to the twin studies, how did outlook relate to health in later life?
options: A positive outlook prevented all signs of physical ageing.
A negative outlook improved health when diet was controlled.
A positive outlook was associated with better later-life health.
Both outlooks produced similar health as the twins grew older.

multipleChoice.question: An older person eats well but has little social contact. What concern follows from the discussion?
options: Diet alone may leave a health-related risk unaddressed.
A healthy diet is likely to cause more loneliness.
Outdoor exercise would certainly remove the risk.
A multigenerational home would be the only solution.

multipleChoice.question: What is the point of describing the Mediterranean way of life beyond its food?
options: To show that its meals are healthier when eaten outdoors.
To show that its benefits may involve exercise and social routines too.
To show that diet matters only in warm countries.
To show that living with relatives replaces the need for exercise.

multipleChoice.question: What can be inferred about the value of communal meals in this discussion?
options: They are valuable mainly because every dish contains fish.
They are valuable only when several generations prepare them.
They guarantee that people will never experience loneliness.
They may support the social contact linked to ageing well.

multipleChoice.question: What is the most reasonable practical message for someone living outside the Mediterranean?
options: Move to a warmer country before changing any daily habits.
Copy Mediterranean meals exactly to gain the same results.
Cultivate a positive outlook and make time for social contact.
Depend mainly on inherited traits to determine future health.
